explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. When the land is divided by lot as an inheritance, the LORD says, "you are to set aside a portion for the LORD, a holy portion of the land…" (Ezekiel 45:1). Before the tribes start squinting at the map for the best spot, a portion is already marked for Him.

Judah is one of Israel's tribes, and the tribes do get their portions of land (Ezekiel 48:8). But the verse here doesn't hand this portion to Judah. It says to set aside "a portion for the LORD." I know Judah sounds like a strong guess, friend, but this slice has a different name on it.

Ephraim is another of Israel's tribes, and it gets a portion in the land too (Ezekiel 48:5). This portion isn't Ephraim's, though. The text says "a portion for the LORD." Nobody's name goes on this one but His.

I see why you'd think some of it is ordinary, baker. But the text doesn't split it up that way. It says, "This entire tract of land will be holy." (Ezekiel 45:1). The whole thing is holy, start to finish.
That's it, baker. Nobody gets to cut this tract into holy parts and ordinary parts. The LORD says, "This entire tract of land will be holy." (Ezekiel 45:1). Every cubit of it counts.

explanations.answer: The priests who minister in the sanctuary
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. This strip is "a holy portion of the land to be used by the priests who minister in the sanctuary, who draw near to minister before the LORD." (Ezekiel 45:4). It's also a place for their houses. The ones who serve nearest the sanctuary get to live nearby.

explanations.answer: The elders who lead the tribes
explanations.explanation: The elders do a lot of leading, but they aren't named in this verse. The strip is for the priests who minister in the sanctuary (Ezekiel 45:4). It holds their houses and the holy area for the sanctuary. No elders are on the list here, friend.

explanations.answer: The prophets who speak for the LORD
explanations.explanation: Prophets get a lot of credit for speaking the LORD's words, and I understand the guess. Still, this verse gives the strip to someone else: "the priests who minister in the sanctuary" (Ezekiel 45:4). Their houses go here too. The prophets aren't mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: The Levites who minister in the temple
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The adjacent area "shall belong to the Levites who minister in the temple" (Ezekiel 45:5). It's their possession, and the towns where they live go there. Priests and Levites end up as neighbors, and I think that sounds like a nice street to live on.

explanations.answer: The judges who rule over the tribes
explanations.explanation: Judges are an interesting guess, friend, but they never show up in these verses. The next strip goes to "the Levites who minister in the temple" (Ezekiel 45:5). They get it for towns to live in. The text names them and nobody else.

explanations.answer: The soldiers who guard the king
explanations.explanation: No soldiers and no king in this part, baker. The text says the strip is for "the Levites who minister in the temple" (Ezekiel 45:5). It's their possession for towns in which to live. The only leader mentioned in these verses is the prince, who comes up soon.

You got it, baker. The city's area is set aside beside the holy district, and "It will belong to the whole house of Israel." (Ezekiel 45:6). It isn't only for the priests, the Levites or the prince. The whole house of Israel shares it.

I get why you doubted it, friend, with so many strips going to specific groups. But this one is different. The text says, "It will belong to the whole house of Israel." (Ezekiel 45:6). Everybody in Israel has a share in it.

Hold on, baker, put the extra land down. The prince does get his own possession, but the text says the princes "will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes." (Ezekiel 45:8). The rest isn't his to keep. It goes to the tribes.

That's right, baker. The prince gets his own possession, and that's where it stops. God says His princes "will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes." (Ezekiel 45:8). No extra helpings for him.

That's the word, friend. God says, "…My princes will no longer oppress My people, but will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes." (Ezekiel 45:8). Oppress means pressing down on people who should be looked after. Under this plan, the prince gives land instead of taking it.

Ignoring people is a real problem, baker, but that's not the word God uses. He says, "…My princes will no longer oppress My people…" (Ezekiel 45:8). Oppressing is worse than ignoring. It means actively pressing down on them. The princes are told to give land to the tribes instead.

Misleading people is sneaky, friend, but this verse is about something heavier. God says, "…My princes will no longer oppress My people…" (Ezekiel 45:8). To oppress is to lean hard on people. Then the princes give the rest of the land to Israel by tribes.

explanations.answer: Do what is just and right
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, "Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right." (Ezekiel 45:9). He doesn't only tell them what to stop. He tells them what to start. And right after that He says, "Stop dispossessing My people."

explanations.answer: Build up the walls of the city
explanations.explanation: Walls are a fine project, friend, but they're not what God asks for here. He tells the princes to "do what is just and right." (Ezekiel 45:9). That's about how they treat people, not about stone and mortar. He also tells them to stop dispossessing His people.

explanations.answer: Gather more land for the temple
explanations.explanation: More land is the opposite direction, baker. The princes are told to "Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right." (Ezekiel 45:9). They're also told to stop dispossessing God's people, which means taking land away from them. God asks for justice, not a bigger lot.

Nailed it, baker. God says, "You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath." (Ezekiel 45:10). An ephah and a bath are measures for dry and liquid goods. If I put my thumb on my cookie scale, every box gets lighter and nobody trusts me. God wants measures that tell the truth.

Heavy scales sound serious, friend, but heavy isn't the word. The text says "honest scales" (Ezekiel 45:10). It's not about how much the scale weighs. It's about whether it tells the truth. A just ephah and a just bath come with it.

Royal sounds fancy, baker, but this verse doesn't ask for fancy. It says, "You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath." (Ezekiel 45:10). Honest means the measure is true, whoever is weighing. Even a prince's goods get weighed on an honest scale.

explanations.answer: All the people of the land
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says, "All the people of the land must participate in this contribution for the prince in Israel." (Ezekiel 45:16). Nobody gets to sit this one out. Everybody brings something to the table.

The priests and Levites have their own strips of land, so I see the guess. But the text says it's all the people. "All the people of the land must participate in this contribution for the prince in Israel." (Ezekiel 45:16). The word "only" doesn't show up anywhere.

explanations.answer: Only the elders of the tribes
explanations.explanation: That would make for a short list, friend. But the text says, "All the people of the land must participate in this contribution for the prince in Israel." (Ezekiel 45:16). It isn't limited to the elders. It's everybody in the land.

explanations.answer: Provide the offerings for the feasts
explanations.explanation: That's the job, baker. "…it shall be the prince’s part to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths…" (Ezekiel 45:17). He also provides the sin offerings and peace offerings. The people bring the contribution, and the prince makes sure the offerings are there.

explanations.answer: Build a palace beside the temple
explanations.explanation: A palace would be a big project, friend, but there's no palace in this passage. The prince's part is to provide the offerings for the feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths (Ezekiel 45:17). That's the job the text gives him.

explanations.answer: Pay the priests their yearly wages
explanations.explanation: Payroll is a real job, baker, but it isn't the one named here. The text gives the prince this part: "to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths…" (Ezekiel 45:17). Wages aren't mentioned in this verse.

That's right, baker. The prince will provide the sin offerings, grain offerings, burnt offerings and peace offerings "to make atonement for the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 45:17). Atonement is the purpose the text names. The offerings are for the whole house of Israel.

I think the long list of offerings made this one tricky, friend. But the text ends the sentence with the purpose: "to make atonement for the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 45:17). So the offerings the prince provides are for atonement. That makes this one true.

You've got it, baker. The Lord GOD says, "…take a young bull without blemish and purify the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 45:18). A young bull without blemish is the offering for it. The first day of the first month starts with the sanctuary being purified.

Welcoming a prince sounds like a party, friend, but the text gives a different purpose. The young bull without blemish is taken to "purify the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 45:18). The prince isn't the reason for this offering.

A harvest blessing is a nice thought, baker, but the text doesn't say that. On the first day of the first month, the young bull is taken to "purify the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 45:18). The sanctuary is what gets purified.

I can see why you'd think so, baker, but the text says the opposite. The seventh-day offering is "for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance." (Ezekiel 45:20). It isn't about people who stray on purpose. It's for people who strayed without meaning to.

That's right, baker. The offering is done "for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance." (Ezekiel 45:20). That's about people who strayed without meaning to. In this way atonement is made for the temple.

Yes, friend. God says, "On the fourteenth day of the first month you are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days, during which unleavened bread shall be eaten." (Ezekiel 45:21). Seven days, with unleavened bread the whole time. That's a long stretch without puffy dough, baker.

The Feast of Weeks is a real feast named in the Law (Exodus 34:22). It isn't the one in this verse, though. This one falls on the fourteenth day of the first month and has unleavened bread. The text names it directly: "the Passover" (Ezekiel 45:21).

The Feast of Harvest is named in the Law too (Exodus 23:16), so it's a fair guess, baker. But the text here says plainly, "you are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days, during which unleavened bread shall be eaten." (Ezekiel 45:21). The fourteenth day of the first month belongs to the Passover.

That's the word, baker. The prince "shall provide a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people of the land." (Ezekiel 45:22). Notice it's for himself too. He's in the same boat as everybody else.

The priests do a lot of work around the offerings, friend, so I see the guess. But the text says the bull is for the prince "and for all the people of the land." (Ezekiel 45:22). It's broader than just the priests. It covers the people of the land.

Elders are a decent guess, baker, but that's not the word in the verse. The prince provides a bull as a sin offering "for himself and for all the people of the land." (Ezekiel 45:22). That takes in everybody, not only the leaders.

explanations.answer: The same offerings as at Passover
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. For the feast that begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, "he is to make the same provision for sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, and oil." (Ezekiel 45:25). Same list, same amounts. No new recipe to learn.

explanations.answer: Twice as many offerings as at Passover
explanations.explanation: Doubling it would be a lot, friend, and my oven would file a complaint. But the text says "the same provision" (Ezekiel 45:25). It's the same as at Passover, not more. Same sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings and oil.

explanations.answer: Only the grain offerings and oil
explanations.explanation: That's cutting the list short, baker. The text says he "is to make the same provision for sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, and oil." (Ezekiel 45:25). So the sin offerings and burnt offerings are included. It's the whole list.
